Author:
fcspartakm
2276A - Perfect Sandwiches
Since each sandwich must contain more cheese than sausage, if $$$b \ge a$$$ then there is definitely no solution.

If $$$a \gt b$$$, let us try to understand the constraints on the number of sandwiches. First, each sandwich must contain at least one piece of sausage, so the number of sandwiches cannot be greater than $$$b$$$. Second, in each sandwich the amount of sausage is smaller than the amount of cheese by at least one piece, so the number of sandwiches cannot be greater than $$$a - b$$$.

It can be shown that these conditions are sufficient, and we can always make $$$k = \min(b, a-b)$$$ sandwiches: first, make $$$k$$$ sandwiches with $$$2$$$ pieces of cheese and $$$1$$$ piece of sausage each. Then $$$a' = a - 2k$$$ pieces of cheese and $$$b' = b - k$$$ pieces of sausage will remain. Since $$$a - b \ge k$$$, we have $$$a' \ge b'$$$, and the remaining pieces can be distributed among the sandwiches either in pairs of the form "one piece of cheese, one piece of sausage" or as separate pieces of cheese.
2276B - Replace and Compress
Author:
BledDest
2276B - Replace and Compress

If the first and last characters of the original string cannot be changed, then the first and last characters of the compressed string also remain unchanged. Since in the compressed string every character differs from the previous one, we are only interested in the possible different lengths of the compressed string that we can obtain: for each length, there is only one compressed string with fixed first and last characters.

In addition, the compressed and uncompressed strings have the same number of pairs of different adjacent characters, and the length of the compressed string depends on it (it is greater by $$$1$$$ than the number of adjacent pairs that differ from each other). Changing one character affects at most two pairs of adjacent characters, so the length of the compressed version can change by at most $$$2$$$.
It also cannot change by exactly $$$1$$$, because we do not change the boundary characters, so the parity of the length is preserved.

This means that it is enough to check whether the length of the compressed version can be increased or decreased by $$$2$$$. To increase the length of the compressed version by $$$2$$$, we need to turn two pairs of equal adjacent characters into two pairs of different ones; that is, in a substring 111 or 000, replace the middle character (and if at least one such substring exists in the string, the answer increases by $$$1$$$). To decrease the length by $$$2$$$, on the contrary, we need to replace the middle character in 101 or 010 (and if at least one such substring exists in the string, the answer also increases by $$$1$$$).
2276C - Subarrays
Author:
fcspartakm
2276C - Subarrays

When working with subarray sums, it's very convenient to use prefix sums: the sum $$$a_l + a_{l+1} + \dots + a_r$$$ is equal to $$$p_r - p_{l-1}$$$, where $$$p_i$$$ is the sum of the first $$$i$$$ elements of the array.

A subarray contributes to the answer if its sum is divisible by $$$k$$$ and its length is greater than $$$k$$$. Thus, for a pair $$$p_i$$$ and $$$p_j$$$ whose difference gives the sum of a subarray, the following conditions must hold:
$$$p_i \bmod k = p_j \bmod k$$$;

Let's construct an array $$$p'$$$ of $$$n+1$$$ numbers, where $$$p'_0 = 0, p'_{i+1} = (p'_i + a_i) \bmod k$$$ (that is, $$$p'_i = p_i \bmod k$$$). In this array, we need to count pairs of equal numbers whose positions differ by more than $$$k$$$.

This can be done using the two-pointer technique. Place the first pointer at the element $$$p'_{k+1}$$$ and the second pointer at the element $$$p'_0$$$. For each $$$j$$$ from $$$0$$$ to $$$k-1$$$, maintain the number of elements equal to $$$j$$$ that have been visited by the second pointer in an auxiliary array $$$cnt$$$. Move the pointers as follows: while the first pointer is still within the array, first process the element at the second pointer (that is, increase its $$$cnt$$$ by $$$1$$$) and move the second pointer to the right. Then, for the element at the first pointer, add its $$$cnt$$$ to the answer (that is, the number of equal elements visited by the second pointer) and move the first pointer to the right.
This solution runs in $$$O(n)$$$. Binary search can be used instead of two pointers, yielding a solution that runs in $$$O(n \log n)$$$.

t = int(input())
for _ in range(t):
    n, k = map(int, input().split())
    a = list(map(int, input().split()))
    
    p = [0 for i in range(n+1)]
    for i in range(n):
        p[i+1] = (p[i]+a[i]) % k

    ans = 0
    cnt = [0 for i in range(k)]
    for i in range(k+1, n+1):
        cnt[p[i-k-1]] += 1
        ans += cnt[p[i]]

    print(ans)
2276D - Caveman
Author:
BledDest
2276D - Caveman

If the graph contains an isolated vertex, there are clearly no valid colorings. Otherwise, we can always construct a valid coloring as follows: in each connected component, choose an arbitrary edge and color one endpoint red and the other blue. Then repeatedly choose an uncolored vertex adjacent to a colored vertex and give it the color opposite to that of the chosen neighbor, until all vertices are colored.

The number of colorings is always even, since we can swap red and blue. Therefore, the answer cannot be $$$1$$$. So, we only need to determine when the answer is $$$2$$$ and when it is greater than $$$2$$$.

If the graph has several connected components, each of them has at least $$$2$$$ valid colorings, and the number of colorings of the entire graph is the product of these numbers over all components. Therefore, if the graph is disconnected, the answer is greater than $$$2$$$.

Otherwise, suppose the graph contains a path on $$$4$$$ vertices. This path alone has at least $$$4$$$ valid colorings: RBRB, BRBR, RBBR, BRRB, and each of them can be extended to a coloring of the entire graph. Therefore, if the graph contains a path on $$$\ge 4$$$ vertices, the answer is greater than $$$2$$$.
If the graph contains a cycle, the answer is also greater than $$$2$$$: a cycle of length $$$4$$$ or more contains a path on $$$4$$$ vertices, while a triangle has at least $$$6$$$ valid colorings.

Thus, a graph with answer $$$2$$$ must be connected, acyclic, and contain no path on $$$4$$$ vertices. This means that it must be a tree with diameter at most $$$2$$$. Every such tree has the following structure: one vertex has degree $$$n-1$$$, and all other vertices are adjacent to it (a star graph). Every such tree has exactly two valid colorings: the color of the central vertex uniquely determines the colors of all other vertices.

Therefore, the answer is $$$2$$$ if and only if the graph is a star. To check this, we can find a vertex with maximum degree and verify that its degree is $$$n-1$$$ and that every other vertex has degree $$$1$$$.
2276E - Good Substrings
Author:
Roms
2276E - Good Substrings
Note: we will use 0-based indexing.

First, let us learn how to build the array $$$nxt[i][d]$$$ — the nearest position $$$j \ge i$$$ where digit $$$d$$$ occurs (or $$$n$$$ if there is no such position). We will build it as follows: we go through the string from right to left and maintain an array $$$cur[0..9]$$$, where $$$cur[d]$$$ is the nearest already seen position of digit $$$d$$$ in the current suffix being considered. At each step $$$i$$$, we update $$$cur[s[i]] = i$$$ and copy $$$cur$$$ into $$$nxt[i]$$$.

Now let us consider what contribution to the answer will be made by substrings with the same left boundary. That is, first we consider the contribution of substrings with $$$l=n - 1$$$, then with $$$l=n-2$$$, and so on.
For the current fixed value of $$$l$$$, let us compute two values $$$r25$$$ and $$$r26$$$:
$$$r25$$$ — the minimum position $$$r$$$ such that the substring $$$s_{l \dots r}$$$ contains the string $$$2025$$$ as a subsequence (or the value $$$n$$$ if there is no such position);
$$$r26$$$ — the minimum position $$$r$$$ such that the substring $$$s_{l \dots r}$$$ contains the string $$$2026$$$ as a subsequence (or the value $$$n$$$ if there is no such position).
We will compute them greedily using the array $$$nxt$$$.
Now what value will all substrings starting at $$$l$$$ add to the answer? Let us consider two cases:
$$$r25 \ge r26$$$ (in this case, all substrings starting at $$$l$$$ are good);
$$$r25 \lt r26$$$ (in this case, the substrings $$$s_{l \dots r25}, s_{l \dots r25 + 1}, \dots, s_{l \dots r26 - 1}$$$ are bad).

First, let us consider the simple case $$$r25 \ge r26$$$. Then for position $$$l$$$ (let us call its contribution $$$ans_l$$$), we need to add $$$n - l$$$ (in 0-based indexing). For $$$ans_{l + 1}$$$, we need to add $$$n - l - 1$$$, and so on.

This can be performed by adding a linear function on a segment. Suppose we have an array and we need to add a linear function to all values on some segment (that is, for every $$$i \in [l, r]$$$, add $$$ki + m$$$ to all values on a segment). We can process it using two arrays: one array will maintain the values of $$$k$$$ added to each position, and another array will maintain the values of $$$m$$$ added.
Now let us consider the case $$$r25 \lt r26$$$. In this case, the string is split into 3 parts:
the substrings $$$s_{l \dots l}, s_{l \dots l + 1}, \dots, s_{l \dots r25 - 1}$$$ are good;
the substrings $$$s_{l \dots r25}, s_{l \dots r25 + 1}, \dots, s_{l \dots r26 - 1}$$$ are bad;
the substrings $$$s_{l \dots r26}, s_{l \dots r26 + 1}, \dots, s_{l \dots n - 1}$$$ are good again;
This can be processed by adding three arithmetic progressions on three different segments: $$$[l, r25-1]$$$; $$$[r25, r26-1]$$$; $$$[r26, n-1]$$$.
To perform addition on segments, you can use difference arrays, Fenwick trees, or segment trees.
2276F - Permutation Coloring Game
Author:
BledDest
2276F - Permutation Coloring Game
To solve this problem, we need to consider the permutation graph. The permutation graph is a directed graph with $$$n$$$ vertices, where each vertex $$$i$$$ has one outgoing edge to vertex $$$p_i$$$.

Since each vertex has exactly one outgoing edge and exactly one incoming edge, the graph decomposes into cycles. To sort a permutation by swapping elements, it is enough to sort each cycle separately: let the vertices of a cycle be $$$v_1, v_2, \dots, v_k$$$ in order; we can swap $$$p_{v_1}$$$ with $$$p_{v_2}$$$, then $$$p_{v_1}$$$ with $$$p_{v_3}$$$, and so on.

This means that, in this problem, if all vertices within each cycle of the permutation have the same color, the permutation can be sorted. On the other hand, if at least one cycle contains two vertices of different colors, it contains two adjacent vertices of different colors, and the number at one of them cannot be moved to the other.
Therefore, Bob's goal is to make some cycle contain vertices of both colors, while Alice's goal is to prevent this.
In the rest of the editorial, we assume that $$$k \ge 2$$$; the case $$$k = 1$$$ must be solved separately (it depends on the length of the longest cycle and the parity of $$$n$$$).

Consider the cycle lengths. If the permutation contains a cycle of length at least $$$k+2$$$, Bob always wins: if Alice is the first to color a vertex in this cycle, Bob can paint another vertex in the opposite color. If Alice does not make a move in this cycle, Bob can color one vertex of the cycle red. After Alice's next turn, at least one uncolored vertex will remain in that same cycle, and Bob can color it blue.

Now only cycles of length $$$k+1$$$ or less remain. If there are at least two cycles of length $$$k+1$$$, Bob wins: if Alice does not make moves in these cycles, Bob can color one vertex in each of them red. After Alice's next turn, at least one of these cycles will still contain an uncolored vertex, which Bob can color blue.

There are two cases left: either there is one cycle of length $$$k+1$$$, or there are none. If there is exactly one cycle of length $$$k+1$$$, Alice must color all cycles of lengths from $$$2$$$ to $$$k$$$ on her first turn: if at least one of them remains, Bob colors one vertex in the cycle of length $$$k+1$$$ and one vertex in the remaining cycle, and Alice cannot color all the uncolored vertices in that cycle on her turn. Let the total length of such cycles be $$$l$$$.

If Alice colors all such cycles, only cycles of length $$$1$$$ and the cycle of length $$$k+1$$$ remain after her turn. Alice's goal is to force Bob to be the first to make a move in this cycle (otherwise, she loses). If the number of cycles of length $$$1$$$ at the start of Bob's turn is divisible by $$$(k+1)$$$, Alice wins: she has a symmetric strategy (if Bob does not color the large cycle but colors $$$b$$$ cycles of length $$$1$$$, Alice can color $$$k+1-b$$$ cycles of length $$$1$$$, making the number of cycles of length $$$1$$$ divisible by $$$(k+1)$$$ again). If this number is not divisible by $$$(k+1)$$$ at the start of Bob's turn, Bob can use the same symmetric strategy against Alice and force her to make a move in the large cycle first. Therefore, if the number of cycles of length $$$1$$$ modulo $$$(k+1)$$$ is $$$c$$$, Alice must color exactly $$$c$$$ such cycles.
If $$$l + c = 0$$$ or $$$l + c \gt k$$$, Alice cannot make a suitable move and loses. Otherwise, she wins using the symmetric strategy described above.

The remaining case is when all cycles have length $$$k$$$ or less. In this case, Alice can color entire cycles, and Bob can win only if, at the start of his turn, there is a set of $$$d \le k$$$ cycles containing at least $$$d + k + 1$$$ vertices in total: he can color one vertex in each of these cycles, and after Alice's next turn, at least one of them will still contain an uncolored vertex. If there is no such set of cycles, Alice can respond to every move by Bob that leaves some cycles partially colored.

Alice's goal is now to make her first move so that no such set of cycles remains. How can we check whether this is possible? Sort the cycles in descending order of length and keep only the $$$2k$$$ longest ones (the others are not worth considering for Bob). Then use dynamic programming: $$$dp_{i,j,x}$$$ means that we have considered the first $$$i$$$ cycles, and Alice has colored $$$j$$$ of them, with a total length of $$$x$$$. The value of the state is the minimum possible sum of $$$(l-1)$$$ over the largest cycles that Bob will take.

The transitions are as follows: either Alice colors the next cycle herself (moving to $$$dp_{i+1, j+1, x+l}$$$, where $$$l$$$ is the length of the next cycle), or she leaves it to Bob (moving to $$$dp_{i+1, j, x}$$$ and adding $$$l-1$$$ to the value if Bob can take one more cycle, that is, if $$$i - j \lt k$$$). If there exists a state $$$dp_{m,j,x} \le k$$$ (where $$$m$$$ is the number of cycles), Alice can choose which cycles to color on her first turn; otherwise, she loses.
This dynamic programming is the most complex part of the solution, and it runs in $$$O(\min(n, k) \cdot k^2)$$$, so the solution comfortably fits within the time limit.
2276G - Elimination of Players
Author:
BledDest
2276G - Elimination of Players

Let $$$F_i$$$ be the number of permutations in which protection takes effect in round $$$i$$$ (that is, player $$$a_i$$$ is the weakest player in round $$$i$$$, but is not eliminated). Also, let $$$G_{i,j}$$$ be the number of permutations in which protection takes effect in round $$$i$$$ and causes player $$$j$$$ to be eliminated. We will learn how to calculate these quantities later; for now, let's show how to get the answer using these values.
Consider when player $$$j$$$ is eliminated in round $$$i$$$ (assuming that $$$a_i \ne j$$$). One of the following situations occurs:
player $$$j$$$ is the weakest remaining player and is not protected;
player $$$j$$$ is the second weakest remaining player, and the weakest player is $$$a_i$$$.

By definition, the number of permutations satisfying the second condition is $$$G_{i,j}$$$. Let us analyze the first condition. Either player $$$j$$$ has strength $$$i$$$, and all players with strength less than $$$i$$$ have already been eliminated, or player $$$j$$$ has strength less than $$$i$$$, but was protected in the previous round.

If player $$$j$$$ was not protected in the previous round, their strength must be $$$i$$$. The number of permutations in which a particular player has strength $$$i$$$ is $$$(n-1)!$$$; however, these also include permutations in which that player is eliminated in the previous round. Therefore, we must subtract $$$G_{i-1, j}$$$ from this number.

If $$$a_{i-1} = j$$$, player $$$j$$$ may have been saved by protection in the previous round; if $$$a_i \ne j$$$, they are eliminated in round $$$i$$$. By definition, the number of permutations satisfying this condition is $$$F_{i-1}$$$.
Thus, for round $$$i \gt 1$$$, the answer for player $$$j$$$ when $$$a_i \ne j$$$ can be calculated as follows:
In this formula, the last term is added only if $$$a_{i-1} = j$$$.
We have expressed the answer in terms of $$$F_i$$$ and $$$G_{i, j}$$$. Now, let's discuss how to calculate them.

How do we calculate $$$F_i$$$? Suppose protection takes effect in round $$$i$$$; this means that player $$$a_i$$$ is the weakest player in that round. Either their strength is $$$i$$$, or their strength is less than $$$i$$$, and they were protected in earlier rounds as well. Let $$$k$$$ be the first round in which protection took effect for this player. Then, in every round from $$$k$$$ to $$$i$$$, the protected player must be $$$a_i$$$, and the strength of player $$$a_i$$$ must be $$$k$$$.

At the first glance, it is sufficient to consider the block of equal values in $$$a$$$ ending at position $$$i$$$. Let its length be $$$l_i$$$; then the strength of player $$$a_i$$$ must be one of $$$l_i$$$ possible values, so there are $$$l_i \cdot (n-1)!$$$ such permutations. However, this is not quite correct: we have not considered the case where player $$$a_i$$$ is eliminated before this block.

When can this happen? Let $$$x$$$ be the beginning of the block (that is, $$$a_x = a_i$$$, but $$$a_{x-1} \ne a_i$$$). If protection took effect in round $$$x-1$$$ and player $$$a_i$$$ had strength $$$x$$$, they would have been eliminated in round $$$x-1$$$. Let us count these cases and subtract them from $$$l_i \cdot (n-1)!$$$.

Let $$$l_{x-1}$$$ be the length of the block of equal values in $$$a$$$ ending at position $$$x-1$$$. If protection took effect in round $$$x-1$$$, the strength of player $$$a_{x-1}$$$ can be one of $$$l_{x-1}$$$ possible values, while player $$$a_i$$$ has strength $$$x$$$. There are $$$l_{x-1} \cdot (n-2)!$$$ such permutations. However, these again include extra permutations: those in which player $$$a_{x-1}$$$ was eliminated before round $$$x-1$$$. We can subtract them in the same way, eventually obtaining an expression resembling inclusion-exclusion:

Let $$$L_0, L_1, \dots$$$ be the lengths of the blocks of equal values up to and including position $$$i$$$ from right to left ($$$L_0 = l_i$$$, $$$L_1 = l_{x-1}$$$, and so on). The number of permutations in which protection takes effect in round $$$i$$$ is

When should we stop this sum? Either when we reach the beginning of the array, or when the next block contains the value that has already appeared in a previously considered block: protection cannot take effect in two blocks with the same $$$a_i$$$ (as soon as the first block ends, the player protected in it is eliminated in the next round). In other words, we stop before a block containing the number that was already encountered.
The block lengths and this sum can easily be updated in $$$O(n)$$$ when moving from $$$i$$$ to $$$i+1$$$.

How do we calculate $$$G_{i,j}$$$? Almost the same way as $$$F_i$$$, but with an additional condition: player $$$j$$$ must have strength $$$(i+1)$$$ (to be eliminated in round $$$i$$$ when protection takes effect). This changes the formula in two ways: first, each factorial involves $$$1$$$ fewer element; second, we must stop the sum as soon as the next block contains player $$$j$$$.

This allows us to calculate each $$$G_{i,j}$$$ in $$$O(n)$$$ time. To reduce this to $$$O(1)$$$, we can build prefix sums of the array $$$[L_0 \cdot (n-2)!, -L_1 \cdot (n-3)!, L_2 \cdot (n-4)!, -L_3 \cdot (n-5)!, \dots]$$$ and, for each $$$j$$$, find the index of the nearest block containing $$$j$$$ (when moving from right to left through array $$$a$$$, starting at position $$$i$$$). This gives a solution in $$$O(n^2)$$$ time.
